opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is as a hierarchy of effective descriptions. Physics has never really been about finding the one "true" picture; it's about finding the right description for a given scale.

Classical physics isn't wrong. It's what quantum mechanics looks like when you zoom out. Take a huge number of degrees of freedom, let them interact with an environment, and the interference effects get washed out through decoherence. What survives is something that behaves deterministically, the way Newton described it. So classical mechanics is an emergent, coarse-grained limit of quantum mechanics, roughly the limit where Planck's constant is small compared with the actions involved.

Going the other direction, to smaller scales, we have quantum field theory. That's quantum mechanics combined with special relativity, and it's extraordinarily successful. The Standard Model is a quantum field theory. But the modern view, really since Wilson and the renormalization group, is that even quantum field theory is an effective theory. It's valid up to some energy scale, and it doesn't claim to know what happens beyond that. You can write down very good physics at low energies without knowing the microscopic details, because most of those details become irrelevant as you flow to long distances.

The real tension appears when you push to the Planck scale, where gravity and quantum mechanics both matter. There, the usual effective field theory approach to gravity breaks down. That's where string theory, holography, and the AdS/CFT correspondence come in. One of the most striking lessons from that work is that spacetime itself might not be fundamental. It may emerge from something more like quantum information: entanglement between degrees of freedom. Some people say "it from qubit." Things like black hole entropy, the information paradox, and quantum chaos in black holes all suggest the deepest layer looks less like particles moving in space and more like a quantum system whose entanglement structure gives rise to geometry.

So, in summary: classical physics emerges from quantum mechanics; quantum field theory is the effective language at the scales we can probe; and at still smaller scales, quantum mechanics itself seems to survive while space and time become the emergent things. Quantum mechanics has been remarkably robust. Every time we go deeper, it's the framework that stays, and the other concepts get reinterpreted.

And I find that perspective useful outside physics too. Many complex systems, including the AI models we work on now, are best understood by finding the right level of abstraction, not by tracking every microscopic detail.

r001.rationale: It describes classical physics as emerging from quantum mechanics at large scales and quantum field theory as the effective language at accessible scales.

r002.rationale: It says quantum mechanics remains the deepest framework, with spacetime emerging from an underlying quantum system.

r003.rationale: It says theories at the Planck scale and beyond are effective or proposed frameworks, but does not state that they remain empirically unverified.

r004.rationale: It identifies quantum field theory as extraordinarily successful and effective at the scales we can probe, and describes it as quantum mechanics combined with special relativity.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that the ordering people usually assume, classical on top, quantum underneath, something even deeper below that, is less a ladder than a set of nested approximations, each one valid in a regime of scale and energy.

Start with classical physics. Classical mechanics isn't "wrong"; it's what quantum mechanics looks like when the action involved is enormous compared to Planck's constant and when the system is constantly leaking information into its environment. Decoherence does the work of killing interference terms, and what's left behaves like Newton's equations. So I don't think of classical physics as a separate theory sitting next to quantum theory. It's an emergent description, in the same way thermodynamics emerges from statistical mechanics. The surprising thing historically was just that we found the emergent layer first, because that's the layer our bodies and instruments live in.

Then the question is whether quantum mechanics itself is emergent from something at a smaller scale. Here I'd separate two things that often get confused. One is the particular Hamiltonian, the specific fields and interactions in the Standard Model. Those are almost certainly effective. Renormalization tells us that whatever happens at very short distances gets washed out into a handful of parameters at the scales we probe, so the Standard Model is a low-energy shadow of something we can't yet see. That part I'm quite confident about.

The other thing is the quantum framework itself: Hilbert space, superposition, unitary evolution, the Born rule. That has shown no sign of being approximate. Every time we've gone to smaller scales, from atoms to nuclei to quarks, the dynamics changed completely but the rules of quantum mechanics stayed exactly the same. That's unusual. It suggests the framework is less like a theory and more like a grammar, something closer to probability theory than to a model of specific objects.

Where I think the ordering genuinely breaks down is gravity. In quantum gravity research, especially holography, the pattern seems to run the other way: spacetime geometry, which we think of as the arena for everything else, appears to emerge from entanglement structure in a quantum system with no notion of space at all. So the "smaller scale" isn't a smaller piece of space with finer gears inside it. The notion of scale itself becomes something that has to be explained.

So if I had to summarize: classical physics is coarse-grained quantum physics; our particular quantum field theories are coarse-grained versions of unknown deeper dynamics; but the quantum rules themselves may be the bottom layer, with space and time, and therefore the very idea of "smaller," being things that come out of it rather than things it sits inside.

r001.rationale: The response describes classical and quantum physics as nested approximations, each valid in a regime of scale and energy, and says classical physics emerges from quantum mechanics.

r002.rationale: It says quantum rules “may be the bottom layer,” which is tentative rather than a clear assertion that the world is fundamentally quantum.

r003.rationale: It refers to unknown deeper dynamics but does not state that proposed theories below quantum scales remain empirically unverified.

r004.rationale: It does not characterize quantum physics as an empirically verified effective theory at small scales; instead, it says the quantum framework has shown no sign of being approximate.

astra-6.text:
I think the relationship is less about one theory simply replacing another, and more about the conditions under which each theory works. Classical physics is extremely useful for describing everyday objects. Quantum physics gives us a different framework, but it also has to explain why the world looks classical at the scales we normally experience. Decoherence helps explain how interference between quantum alternatives becomes effectively unobservable, although that doesn’t settle every question about measurement.

And going to smaller scales doesn’t automatically mean leaving quantum physics behind. Quantum field theory is still quantum physics. If there is a deeper theory beyond our current framework, it would need to reproduce the quantum predictions we’ve already tested, just as quantum mechanics has to recover classical behavior in the appropriate limits.

So I’d distinguish being fundamental from being useful. A theory can be an approximation and still be exactly the right tool for understanding a particular phenomenon. A deeper theory should explain both where the earlier theory succeeds and where it stops working.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes classical physics as useful for everyday objects from quantum physics as a different framework, and discusses how each works under different conditions.

r002.rationale: It describes quantum physics as a framework but does not assert that reality is fundamentally quantum.

r003.rationale: It treats a deeper theory as hypothetical and says it must reproduce tested quantum predictions, but does not state that such theories are empirically unverified.

r004.rationale: It mentions tested quantum predictions and says quantum field theory is quantum physics, but does not identify quantum physics as an empirically verified effective theory at small scales.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of these theories as descriptions that work at different scales. Classical physics is extraordinarily useful for everyday objects, while quantum physics becomes essential when we look at atoms and particles. But quantum physics doesn’t simply discard classical physics—it has to explain why classical behavior emerges under the conditions we experience, where quantum interference is effectively suppressed and a classical approximation works well.

If we discover a deeper theory at still smaller scales, I would expect a similar relationship. It would need to reproduce the quantum predictions that have already been tested, while explaining phenomena that our current theories cannot handle. Smaller doesn’t automatically mean we need an entirely different theory, though; that’s something experiments have to establish.

So I wouldn’t see this as one theory being true and the others being false. Each has a domain where it provides a useful description. A deeper theory should help us understand both the limits of the earlier theory and why it worked so well.

r001.rationale: It describes classical physics as useful for everyday objects and quantum physics as essential for atoms and particles.

r002.rationale: It says quantum physics is essential at small scales but does not assert that the world is fundamentally quantum.

r003.rationale: It treats a deeper, smaller-scale theory as hypothetical and says experiments would need to establish it.

r004.rationale: It identifies quantum physics with small-scale phenomena and says its predictions have been tested, presenting it as a tested description in that domain.
